lessons.title: Where our food comes from

context: Daniel talks to Maya about food at work.
We buy farm to table food at the market. It tastes fresh.
dialogue: Daniel: Maya, where does our food come from?
Maya: Most of it comes from farms near the town.
Daniel: What grows in the orchard on the hill?
Maya: Apples grow in the orchard, and grapes grow in a vineyard by the river.
Daniel: What about the cows in the pasture?
Maya: They give milk and cheese. We buy farm to table food at the market.
lessons.listening: On Monday, Daniel talks to Maya about food. He asks, 'Maya, where does our food come from?' Maya says, 'Most of it comes from farms near the town. Apples grow in an orchard on the hill, and grapes grow in a vineyard by the river. Cows feed in a pasture near the lake.' Daniel says, 'Thank you, Maya.'
lessons.question: Where does the food come from?
lessons.reading: On Monday, Daniel talks to Maya about food at Carter Retail Group. He says, 'Where does our food come from?' Maya says, 'Most of it comes from farms near the town. Apples grow in an orchard on the hill, and grapes grow in a vineyard by the river. Cows feed in a pasture near the lake.' Daniel says, 'I like food that is farm to table. It tastes fresh.' Maya says, 'Yes. At a farmers' market, you can meet the people who grow your food. They sell apples from the orchard, and cheese from cows in the pasture. The vineyard sells grape juice, too.' Daniel says, 'Good. I want to buy food at a farmers' market every week. Farm to table food is fresh, and it helps local farms. An orchard, a vineyard and a pasture are the start of every meal.' Maya says, 'That is true. Good food starts on a good farm.'
lessons.readingA: In an orchard on the hill.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about where your food comes from. What do you buy?

Apples grow in an orchard on the hill, and grapes grow in a vineyard by the river. Cows feed in a pasture near the lake.' I buy farm to table food at a farmers' market.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend. Tell them where your food comes from.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Tom, I want to tell you about where my food comes from. On Monday, Daniel talked about food at work. He said, 'Where does our food come from?' Maya said, 'Most of it comes from farms near the town. Apples grow in an orchard on the hill, and grapes grow in a vineyard by the river. Cows feed in a pasture near the lake.' dialogue: Priya: Daniel, how do farmers grow so much food?
Daniel: Many farms use pesticide to kill insects.
Priya: What is fertilizer?
Daniel: Fertilizer helps plants grow, and irrigation brings water to dry fields.
Priya: What about organic farming?
Daniel: Organic farming uses no pesticide. Free-range eggs come from hens outside.

Daniel says, 'Many farms use pesticide to kill insects, and fertilizer to help plants grow. Irrigation brings water to dry fields.' Priya says, 'What about organic farming?' Daniel says, 'Organic farming uses no pesticide and no chemical fertilizer. It uses natural ways to keep the soil rich.' Priya says, 'Is the food better?' Free-range eggs come from hens outside. Good farming feeds people.

context: Maya talks to Daniel about food miles at work.
When we shop locally, food miles stay low.
dialogue: Maya: Daniel, what are food miles?
Daniel: Food miles are the distance food travels to reach us.
Maya: What is traceability?
Daniel: Traceability lets us follow food from farm to fork.
Maya: What about wholesale?
Daniel: Wholesale means shops buy food in large amounts. When we shop locally, food miles stay low.
lessons.listening: On Wednesday, Maya talks to Daniel about food miles at work. She asks, 'Daniel, what are food miles?' Daniel says, 'Food miles are the distance food travels to reach us. When we shop locally, food miles stay low.' Maya asks, 'What is traceability?' Daniel says, 'It lets us follow food from farm to fork.' Maya is happy.
lessons.question: What are food miles?
lessons.reading: On Wednesday, Maya talks to Daniel about food miles at work. She says, 'Food miles are the distance food travels to reach us.' Daniel says, 'Apples from far away have high food miles. When we shop locally, food miles stay low.' Maya says, 'What is traceability?' Daniel says, 'Traceability lets us follow food from farm to fork. We can see where it grew and how it travelled.' Maya says, 'And wholesale?' Daniel says, 'Wholesale means shops buy food in large amounts. A small shop can still buy from local farms.' Maya says, 'So local food is better?' Daniel says, 'Yes. When we shop locally, we follow food from farm to fork, and traceability is easy. Food miles stay low, and farmers near us earn a fair price.' Maya says, 'Good. I will shop locally this week.'
lessons.readingQ: What does traceability let us do?
lessons.readingA: Follow food from farm to fork.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about food miles. Why buy local food?

Daniel said, 'Apples from far away have high food miles. When we shop locally, food miles stay low.' Traceability lets us follow food from farm to fork. Wholesale means shops buy food in large amounts.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend. Tell them about food miles.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Tom, I want to tell you about food miles. On Wednesday, Maya talked about food miles at work. She said, 'Food miles are the distance food travels to reach us.' Daniel said, 'Apples from far away have high food miles. When we shop locally, food miles stay low.' Traceability lets us follow food from farm to fork. Wholesale means shops buy food in large amounts. I like local food. Please tell me about your food. Best, Daniel
lessons.sound: Traceability has its strongest beat on BIL. In traceability, say BIL clearly in the middle. In wholesale, say WHOLE clearly at the start.
lessons.model: Good traceability helps us trust our food.

context: Daniel meets Sara at a farmers' market and talks about food.
A food bank gives free food to people in need.
dialogue: Daniel: Sara, do you know what a food bank is?
Sara: Yes. A food bank gives free food to people in need.
Daniel: What is food insecurity?
Sara: It is not having enough food to live well.
Daniel: What is a food desert?
Sara: It is an area with no shops selling fresh food. Famine and malnutrition are big problems.

lessons.question: What is a food bank?
lessons.correct: It gives free food to people in need
lessons.reading: On Monday, Daniel meets Sara at a farmers' market and talks about food. He asks, 'Sara, do you know what a food bank is?' Sara says, 'Yes. A food bank gives free food to people in need.' Daniel asks, 'What is food insecurity?' Sara says, 'It is not having enough food to live well. In a food desert, there are no shops with fresh food.' Daniel says, 'That is sad.' Sara says, 'Yes. Famine is a serious lack of food in a large area, and malnutrition makes children weak.' Daniel says, 'How can we help?' Sara says, 'A food bank helps today. Food insecurity needs long plans. In a food desert, a small shop can change lives. Famine and malnutrition are big problems, but good food can start to fix them.'
lessons.readingA: Not having enough food to live well.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about food and helping people. What is a food bank?
lessons.speakingSample: I want to tell you about food and helping people. On Monday, Daniel talked to Sara at a farmers' market. He said, 'Sara, do you know what a food bank is?' Sara said, 'Yes. A food bank gives free food to people in need.' Food insecurity is not having enough food to live well. In a food desert, there are no shops with fresh food.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend. Tell them about food and helping people.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Tom, I want to tell you about food and helping people. On Monday, Daniel talked to Sara at a farmers' market. He said, 'Sara, do you know what a food bank is?' Sara said, 'Yes. A food bank gives free food to people in need.' Food insecurity is not having enough food to live well. In a food desert, there are no shops with fresh food. Famine and malnutrition are big problems. Please tell me about your town. Best, Daniel
lessons.sound: Famine has its strongest beat on FAM. In famine, say FAM clearly at the start. In malnutrition, say TRI clearly in the middle.
lessons.model: A famine hits the whole country.

transferCheck.source: On Saturday, Sara reads a note from her neighbour about a community garden. It says the garden grows food for a food bank, and many families in the town use it. Food insecurity is a big problem here, but the garden helps. Sara talks to her friend Tom at a farmers' market. She says, 'The garden grows food for a food bank. Good food can start to fix big problems.' Tom says, 'Good. A small shop can change lives.' Sara says, 'Yes. In a food desert, fresh food is hard to find, but the garden helps.' Tom says, 'Good. A food bank helps today.' Sara is happy.
transferCheck.dictation: Good food starts on a good farm.
